Definition of Finance
Finance is the study of the management, movement, and raising of money. The word finance can be used as a
verb, such as when the First National Bank agrees to finance your home mortgage loan. It can also be used as
a noun referring to an entire industry. At its essence, the study of finance is about understanding the uses and
sources of cash, as well as the concept of risk-reward trade-off. Finance is also a tool that can help us be better
decision makers.
Basic Areas in Finance
Finance is divided into three primary areas in the domestic market: business finance, investments, and
financial markets and institutions (see Figure 1.2). We look at each here in turn.
Figure 1.2 The Three Basic Areas of Study in Finance
Business Finance
Business finance looks at how managers can apply financial principles to maximize the value of a firm in a
risky environment. Businesses have many stakeholders. In the case of corporations, the shareholders own the
company, and they hire managers to run the company with the intent to maximize shareholder wealth.

Capital budgeting is the process of determining which long-term or fixed assets to acquire in an effort to
maximize shareholder value. Capital budgeting decisions add the greatest value to a firm. As such, capital
budgeting is thought to be one of the most important financial functions within a firm. The capital
budgeting process consists of estimating the value of potential investments by forecasting the size,
timing, and risk of cash flows associated with the investments. The finance department develops and
compiles cash flow estimates with input from the marketing, operations, accounting, human resources,
and economics departments to develop a portfolio of investment projects that collectively maximize the
value of the firm.

The Great Recession
The Great Recession of 2007–2009 exposed many of the weaknesses of our financial system. The ease with
which banks could lower credit standards to allow ill-prepared consumers to purchase real estate and the
resulting speed with which the world economy plunged into recession is astounding.
Regulation to address the economic crisis was also swift. Fortunately, Ben Bernanke, chairman of the
Federal Reserve at the time, had throughout his career conducted extensive research into the causes of and
potential resolution of the Great Depression of the 1930s.2 He was uniquely qualified to lead the economic
response to the crisis. Some resulting laws moved to address the immediate needs and others to correct
the underlying causes of the recession.
One immediate fix was the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP). TARP authorized the Treasury to buy
illiquid assets in order to save the financial institutions so important to lubricating our economy. Politically
this was a tough decision, as it appeared that the government bailed out greedy bankers. In the end,
however, the program was justified because the economy immediately began a slow but steady recovery,

Finance is the lubricant that keeps our economy running smoothly. Issuing a mortgage can be profitable for a
bank, but it also allows people to live in their own homes and to pay for them over time. Do MasterCard,
Venmo, and PayPal make money when you use their product? Sure, but think how much more convenient and
safer it is to carry a card or use an app instead of cash. In addition, these services allow you to easily track
where and how you spend your money. A well-regulated and independent financial system is important to
capital-based economies. Our smoothly functioning financial system has removed us from the days of strictly
bartering to our system today, where transactions are as simple as a tap on your mobile phone.

At its most basic level, risk is uncertainty. The study of finance attempts to quantify risk in a way that helps
individuals and organizations assess an appropriate trade-off for risk. Risk-return tradeoffs are all around us in
our everyday decision-making. When we consider walking across the street in the middle of a city block or
walking down to the marked intersection, we are assessing the trade-off between convenience and safety.
Should you buy the required text for your class or instead rely on the professor’s notes and the internet?

assess the vehicle before you buy? Should you accept your first job offer at graduation or hold out for the offer

qa_pairs.question: What is a risk-return tradeoff?

This tradeoff is all around us in our everyday decision-making. For example, when deciding whether to buy the required text for a class or rely on the professor's notes and the internet, one is assessing the trade-off between the cost of the textbook and the potential benefits of having the physical text. Similarly, when deciding whether to buy a used car sight unseen or spend money for a mechanic to assess the vehicle before buying, one is weighing the convenience of immediate purchase against the potential costs of unforeseen repairs.

Importance of Data
Financial data is important for internal and external analysis of business firms. More accurate and timely data
leads to better business and financial decision-making. Financial budgeting and forecasting rely on the
creation of several types of financial statements including income statements, the statements of cash flow,
and balance sheets, as well as the notes and assumptions used to create the financial statements. Insiders
such as executive and middle managers use financial data to evaluate and reevaluate decision-making. Having
current and accurate data is key to making consistent value-adding decisions for a firm. Data helps inform
managers about how and when to finance projects, which projects to undertake, and necessary changes to
make regarding physical, financial, and human resource assets. “Gut feelings” and “seat-of-the-pants”
decision-making tend to be inconsistent with value maximization.

Microeconomics focuses on individual units such as households and firms, while macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole, including areas like inflation, income, economic growth, and unemployment.

qa_pairs.question: Why is it important for a firm like Bacon Signs to consider macroeconomic factors when planning to expand its business?
qa_pairs.answer: Bacon Signs had to consider unemployment and inflation when estimating its price of labor and materials, and interest rates when estimating the cost of borrowing money to expand the business. This is because macroeconomic factors like unemployment, inflation, and interest rates can significantly impact the cost of production and the demand for the firm's products, which are crucial factors in business expansion.

qa_pairs.question: Why is macroeconomic modeling limited in its application?
qa_pairs.answer: Macroeconomic modeling is limited because models cannot capture every variable in testing and application. This means that while models can provide useful insights and predictions, they may not account for all the complexities and nuances of the real-world economy, leading to inaccuracies in their results.

qa_pairs.question: Why is it necessary to incorporate macroeconomic assumptions and expectations into individual firm and industry forecasts?
qa_pairs.answer: Financial forecasting must incorporate macroeconomic assumptions and expectations into individual firm and industry forecasts because the economy as a whole can have a significant impact on the performance of individual firms and industries. For example, changes in interest rates, inflation, or unemployment can affect the demand for a firm's products, the cost of production, and the cost of borrowing money, all of which can impact the firm's financial performance.

To make financial forecasts, managers need good information to understand the relationship among several
economic variables. Working from small to large, sales forecasts estimate the likely price and quantity of
goods sold. In doing so, the forecaster will consider local, regional, state, national, and international economic
conditions. Inflation is an important macroeconomic variable that influences prices. Every quarter, financial
information hubs, such as the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), and government agencies and regulatory bodies, such
as the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve, release estimates about expected and current inflation.
This information informs policy makers how to adjust the money supply to meet target objectives. Financial
forecasters pay close attention to current and expected interest rates, as they have a fundamental impact on
the cost of raising money and determining the required rate of return for investment.

instruments into debt instruments traded in the bond markets and equity securities traded on the stock
markets.
The federal government issues Treasury notes and bonds to raise money for current spending and to repay
past borrowing. The size of the Treasury market is quite large, as the US federal government over the years
has accumulated a total indebtedness of over $28 trillion.10

Definition of Economic Value
Value is a term used frequently in business and especially in economics, accounting, and finance. Accountants
track, record, and display value in the form of financial statements and footnotes. The numbers they present
are “book values” and represent what has occurred. Financial people like to speak in terms of “market values.”
Market values are calculated using expected future cash flows discounted to today. Market values are the
prices that consumers pay for a product. Economic value is what we believe consumers are actually willing to
pay for a product, service, or experience. For example, the price of a movie ticket may be $10, but there are
individuals who are willing to pay far more for the experience of watching a movie on the big screen.

qa_pairs.question: What is capital budgeting and why is it important for a firm?
qa_pairs.answer: Capital budgeting is the process of determining which long-term or fixed assets to acquire in an effort to maximize shareholder value. It is crucial for a firm as it helps in making strategic decisions about the allocation of financial resources over a long period, ensuring that the investments made in assets will generate sufficient returns to meet the organization's objectives.

qa_pairs.question: What is the capital market and what types of financial instruments does it deal with?
qa_pairs.answer: The capital market is a market for longer-term financial instruments, such as stocks and bonds, used to finance long-term projects for organizations. It deals with securities that are issued for periods longer than one year, providing funds for the firm's long-term needs.

qa_pairs.question: What is the role of a chief financial officer (CFO) in a firm?
qa_pairs.answer: The chief financial officer (CFO) is an executive-level officer who sets policy for working capital management, determines optimal capital structure for the firm, and makes the final decision in matters of capital budgeting. They are responsible for the financial health of the organization and play a key role in strategic decision-making.

qa_pairs.question: What is commercial paper (CP) and what is it used for?
qa_pairs.answer: Commercial paper (CP) is a short-term, unsecured financial obligation issued by firms as a means of short-term financing for items such as inventory or payables. It is a popular tool for companies to raise funds quickly and efficiently, as it matures within 270 days.

qa_pairs.question: What is the role of a comptroller in a firm?
qa_pairs.answer: A comptroller, also referred to as controller, is an individual in charge of financial reporting and the oversight of the accounting activities necessary to develop financial reports. They are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of financial records, and for providing financial information to management and other stakeholders.

qa_pairs.question: What is a dealer in the context of financial markets?
qa_pairs.answer: A dealer is an entity that facilitates a market and the trading of securities by holding a portfolio of the underlying asset for easy purchase and sale. They earn money on the spread between ask and bid prices for the asset, acting as a middleman in the buying and selling process.

qa_pairs.question: What is default risk and why is it important?
qa_pairs.answer: Default risk is the risk that the issuer of a financial security will be unable to make payments as specified in the terms of the security. It is important because it can lead to financial losses for investors and can have a negative impact on the overall stability of the financial market.

qa_pairs.answer: The Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) is a nonprofit corporation that provides brokerage customers up to $500,000 coverage for cash and securities held by the firm. qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between the primary market and the secondary market in financial markets?
qa_pairs.answer: The primary market is the market for the purchase and sale of new securities, while the secondary market represents the purchase or sale of used securities that trade after the initial sale by the offering firm. In other words, the primary market is where new securities are first issued and sold, while the secondary market is where these securities are traded among investors after they have been initially sold.

qa_pairs.question: What are Treasury bills (T-bills), Treasury bonds, and Treasury notes, and how do they differ?
qa_pairs.answer: Treasury bills (T-bills) are short-term debt obligations of one year or less issued by the US government. Treasury bonds are long-term debt obligations issued by the US government characterized by having maturities of greater than 10 years and making periodic interest payments as well as principal payment at maturity. Treasury notes are similar to Treasury bonds, but they have maturities between 2 and 10 years. In other words, T-bills are short-term securities, Treasury notes are intermediate-term securities, and Treasury bonds are long-term securities.

qa_pairs.question: What is the role of a financial analyst in a financial institution?
qa_pairs.answer: A financial analyst in a financial institution such as a bank or investment company plays a crucial role in providing financial advice to businesses and individuals. They analyze financial data, create forecasts, and develop investment strategies to help their clients make informed decisions. They also assess the financial health of companies by reviewing their financial statements, ratios, and other key performance indicators. Additionally, they may conduct risk analysis to identify potential threats and opportunities for their clients.

qa_pairs.question: Is a dealer or a broker more likely to be a market maker? What activities does a market maker perform?
qa_pairs.answer: A dealer is more likely to be a market maker. A market maker is a participant in a financial market who quotes both a buy and a sell price for a security, and is ready to buy or sell that security at any time. They provide liquidity to the market by buying and selling securities to facilitate trades between buyers and sellers. Market makers also take on the risk of holding an inventory of securities to ensure that there is always a buyer or a seller available. They make profits by earning the bid-ask spread, which is the difference between the price at which they buy and the price at which they sell.

qa_pairs.question: How can an understanding of micro- and macroeconomic factors aid in small business decision-making?
qa_pairs.answer: Understanding micro- and macroeconomic factors can help small businesses make informed decisions by providing insights into the current and future economic environment. Microeconomic factors, such as consumer behavior, competition, and supply and demand, can help businesses understand their target market, pricing strategies, and production levels. Macroeconomic factors, such as interest rates, inflation, and government policies, can help businesses anticipate changes in the overall economy and adjust their strategies accordingly. For example, if a business anticipates an increase in interest rates, it may choose to borrow less money or delay investments. Understanding these factors can help businesses make more informed decisions and increase their chances of success.

qa_pairs.question: Why does the company with the lower sales level have greater market capitalization?
qa_pairs.answer: A company with a lower sales level may have greater market capitalization if its stock is highly valued by investors. This can happen for several reasons. For example, the company may have strong earnings, a promising future growth potential, or a unique product or service that sets it apart from its competitors. Additionally, the company may have a low price-to-earnings ratio, which means that its stock is undervalued relative to its earnings. This can attract investors who believe that the stock will increase in value over time. It's also possible that the company has a large number of outstanding shares, which can dilute the value of each share and lower its market capitalization. However, it's important to note that market capitalization is just one measure of a company's value, and it's important to consider other factors as well.

Why It Matters
When someone opens a business, it is because they want to fulfill important personal financial goals. In
publicly traded companies, managers and employees work on behalf of the shareholders, who own the
business through their ownership of company stock. These managers and employees have an ongoing
obligation to pursue projects, policies, and corporate investments that will increase or promote stockholder
value over the long term. Although many companies focus on financially related goals, such as growth,

Corporations
The most common type of organizational structure for larger businesses is the corporation. A corporation is a
legal business entity that is created under the laws of a state. This entity operates separately and distinctly
from its owners and managers. It is the separation of the corporate entity from its owners and managers that
limits stockholders’ losses to the amount they originally invest in the firm. In other words, a corporation can
lose all of its money and go bankrupt, but its owners will only lose the funds that they originally invested in the
company.
Unlike other forms of organization, corporations have unlimited lives as business entities. It is far easier to
transfer shares of stock in a corporation than it is to transfer one’s interest in an unincorporated business.
These factors make it much easier for corporations to raise the capital necessary to operate large businesses.

qa_pairs.question: What are the advantages of a corporation as a business structure compared to other forms of organization?
qa_pairs.answer: A corporation has several advantages as a business structure compared to other forms of organization. Firstly, it operates separately and distinctly from its owners and managers, which limits stockholders’ losses to the amount they originally invest in the firm. This means that even if a corporation goes bankrupt, its owners will only lose the funds that they originally invested in the company. Secondly, corporations have unlimited lives as business entities, making them more stable and long-lasting. Lastly, it is much easier to transfer shares of stock in a corporation than it is to transfer one’s interest in an unincorporated business, making it easier for corporations to raise the capital necessary to operate large businesses.

A shareholder or stockholder can be a person, company, or organization that holds stock in a given company.

Functions of a Board of Directors
A board of directors is a group of people who are elected to represent shareholders, and these directors are
then ultimately responsible for running the company. Every public company is legally required to install a
board of directors. Nonprofit organizations and many private companies often establish a board of directors
as well, even if they are not legally required to do so.
The board is responsible for protecting shareholders’ interests, establishing management policies, overseeing
the corporation or organization, and making decisions about important issues. The board of directors acts as a
fiduciary for shareholders. The board is also tasked with a number of other responsibilities, including setting
company goals, creating dividend and stock option policies, hiring and firing chief executive officers (CEOs),
and ensuring that the company has the resources it needs to perform well.

They act as a fiduciary for shareholders, setting company goals, creating dividend and stock option policies, hiring and firing chief executive officers (CEOs), and ensuring that the company has the resources it needs to perform well.

qa_pairs.question: What is an independent board member?
qa_pairs.answer: An independent board member is a member of a board of directors who is not affiliated with any other significant business relationship with the company, such as being a major shareholder or an executive officer. qa_pairs.question: What are the arguments for and against having independent board members?
qa_pairs.answer: Arguments for having independent board members include the ability to provide objective and unbiased judgment, to challenge management decisions, and to bring diverse perspectives and expertise to the board. Arguments against having independent board members include the potential for lack of familiarity with the company's operations and culture, and the potential for increased costs associated with hiring and compensating independent directors.

qa_pairs.question: How can boards become diverse?

Basic Structure of a Board of Directors
The bylaws of a company or organization determine the structure, responsibilities, and powers given to a
board of directors. The bylaws also determine how many board members there are, how the members are
elected, and how frequently the board members meet.
The board must represent shareholder and management interests, so it is best for the board to include both
internal and external members. Usually, there is an internal director and an external director. The internal
director is a member of the board who is involved with the daily workings of the company and manages the
interests of shareholders, officers, and employees. The external director represents the interests of those who
function outside of the company. The CEO often serves as the chairman of the company’s board of directors.

Corporate governance is a discipline that focuses on how a company conducts its business and the various
controls that are implemented to ensure proper procedures and ethical behavior.
Although many companies and managers do operate with a fair and honest philosophy, others will try to
exploit the temporary benefits of actions that fall outside ethical behavior. Companies do not always adhere to

Importance of Improving Oversight and Governance
It is crucial to today’s corporate environment that firms do not lose sight of achieving and maintaining strong
and efficient oversight and governance. This is true despite the litany of other important items on the busy
agendas of most boards.
Keeping a focus on the critical ethics of management, as well as the traditional focus on the importance of
ethics to the overall organization, is not only timely in this day and age but also sound business practice. The
importance of establishing a comprehensive system of checks and balances cannot be overemphasized.
Beginning with the chief executive officer, these checks and balances need to progress through senior
management, and they ultimately include the board of directors itself. Similar checks and balances need to
then filter down though the rest of the entire firm. By taking the appropriate steps to improve corporate
oversight and governance, overall business risk can be mitigated and future operational problems reduced.
Additionally, such steps can lead to the positive effects of achieving sustainable operational and financial
benefits for a company and its shareholders.

Agency problems refers to conflicts that occur when an agent (manager) who is entrusted with following the
interests of the principal (shareholder or owner) of an organization abuses their position to further their own

irrespective of it being a church, a club, a not-for-profit organization, a multinational corporation, or any other
government agency or institution. As with most problematic issues in business, agency problems can be
resolved, but only if organizations are willing to take the appropriate steps to resolve them.

operations are not being adversely impacted by the agency problem.

Domestic companies operate completely or for the most part within the borders of the United States. While

subsidiaries of such international firms may be regulated by laws dictated by their host countries. These will
often differ significantly from those in the United States.

qa_pairs.question: Who is considered an agent in a business context?
qa_pairs.answer: In a business context, an agent is a person who acts on behalf of another person or group. This could be a company executive acting on behalf of the shareholders, a lawyer acting on behalf of a client, or a real estate agent acting on behalf of a property seller.

qa_pairs.question: What is an annual meeting and why is it important?
qa_pairs.answer: An annual meeting is a meeting of the general membership and shareholders of a corporation, also known as an annual general meeting (AGM). It is an important event because it provides an opportunity for shareholders to discuss the corporation's operations, financial condition, and future plans, and to vote on important matters such as the election of directors and the approval of the annual report.

qa_pairs.question: What is an annual report and what is its purpose?
qa_pairs.answer: An annual report is a document describing a public corporation’s operations and financial condition that must be provided to shareholders once per year. It is an important tool for shareholders to understand the corporation's performance and financial health, and to make informed decisions about their investment. In the United States, the annual report is also known as Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Form 10-K.

qa_pairs.question: What are articles of incorporation and what is their purpose?
qa_pairs.answer: Articles of incorporation are a set of formal documents filed with a government body to legally document the creation of a corporation. They outline the corporation's name, purpose, structure, and other important details such as the number and rights of the shares that can be issued. They are an essential part of the process of forming a corporation and are required to legally establish the corporation's existence.

qa_pairs.question: What is a board of directors (BOD) and what is its role?
qa_pairs.answer: A board of directors (BOD) is a group of people who jointly supervise the activities of an organization, such as a corporation. They are responsible for making major decisions about the direction and strategy of the organization, and for ensuring that it is being run in a manner that is in the best interests of its shareholders. They are elected by the shareholders and are accountable to them for the performance of the organization.

qa_pairs.question: What is a C corporation and how is it taxed?
qa_pairs.answer: A C corporation is a legal structure for a corporation in which the owners, or shareholders, are taxed separately from the entity. This means that the corporation is considered a separate tax-paying entity, and the shareholders are taxed on their dividends and any capital gains they may realize from the sale of their shares. This structure is commonly used for large, publicly traded corporations.

qa_pairs.question: What is a close (closely held) corporation and how is it different from a C corporation?
qa_pairs.answer: A close (closely held) corporation is a company that has only a limited number of shareholders. It is different from a C corporation in that it is not publicly traded, and the shares are not easily transferable. This structure is commonly used for small, family-owned businesses or businesses with a small number of investors.

qa_pairs.question: What is a conference call and how is it used in a business context?
qa_pairs.answer: A conference call is a meeting or presentation conducted via telephone or internet to relay company information to a group of people. It is commonly used in a business context to communicate with employees, shareholders, or other stakeholders who are located in different geographic locations. It allows for efficient and convenient communication, and can save time and resources compared to traditional in-person meetings.

2. Limited Liability Partnership (LLP): This is a partnership in which some or all partners have limited liabilities. It can exhibit elements of both partnerships and corporations.

Non-stock corporation: This is a corporation that does not have owners represented by shares of stock but typically has members who are the functional equivalent of stockholders in a stock corporation (having the right to vote, etc.). qa_pairs.answer: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is a large, independent agency of the United States federal government. qa_pairs.question: Who are the secretaries of state and what is their role?

qa_pairs.question: What is a sole proprietor and sole proprietorship?
qa_pairs.answer: A sole proprietor is an individual who owns an unincorporated business entirely by themselves. The owner has unlimited liability for all obligations and debts of the business.

qa_pairs.question: What is the most important document required to form a corporation?
qa_pairs.answer: The most important document required to form a corporation is the Articles of Incorporation. This document outlines the basic framework for the corporation, including its name, purpose, stock structure, and the rights and responsibilities of its shareholders.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a shareholder and a stakeholder?
qa_pairs.answer: A shareholder is an individual or entity that owns shares of stock in a corporation. They have a financial stake in the company and are entitled to a portion of its profits, if any, in the form of dividends. A stakeholder, on the other hand, is any individual or entity that has an interest in the success of the corporation, whether financial or not. This can include employees, customers, suppliers, and even the community in which the corporation operates.

qa_pairs.question: What group within a corporation has the primary responsibility for protecting the interests of shareholders?
qa_pairs.answer: The board of directors has the primary responsibility for protecting the interests of shareholders. qa_pairs.question: What are three essential best practices in corporate governance and why are they important?
qa_pairs.answer: Three essential best practices in corporate governance are separation of duties, the need for non-executive directors, and the importance of a non-executive audit committee. Separation of duties helps to prevent fraud and errors by ensuring that no single individual has complete control over a critical process. Non-executive directors provide an independent perspective and help to ensure that the company is being run in the best interests of all stakeholders. They are not involved in the day-to-day operations of the company and can provide a fresh perspective on strategic decisions. A non-executive audit committee is responsible for overseeing the financial reporting and accounting processes of the company to ensure accuracy and compliance with laws and regulations. These best practices are important because they help to prevent fraud, ensure the company's financial stability, and promote ethical behavior.

qa_pairs.question: Why is corporate governance an ongoing process that must continuously be evaluated by a company?
qa_pairs.answer: Corporate governance is an ongoing process that must continuously be evaluated by a company because the business environment is constantly changing, and the company must adapt to these changes to remain competitive. The company's goals, strategies, and operations may change over time, and the board of directors must ensure that the company's governance structure is aligned with these changes. Additionally, new laws and regulations may be introduced, and the company must ensure that it is in compliance with these changes. The board of directors must also continuously evaluate the effectiveness of the company's governance structure to ensure that it is promoting ethical behavior, preventing fraud, and ensuring the company's financial stability.

qa_pairs.question: What is meant by LEARR in the context of governance codes and why are its components important to a company’s continuing operations?
qa_pairs.answer: LEARR is an acronym that stands for Leadership, Ethics, Accountability, Risk, and Remuneration in the context of governance codes. These components are important to a company's continuing operations because they help to ensure that the company is being run ethically, accountably, and in a way that minimizes risk. Leadership refers to the board's role in setting the company's strategic direction and ensuring that it is aligned with the company's goals. Ethics refers to the company's commitment to acting in an ethical manner and promoting ethical behavior throughout the organization. Accountability refers to the board's responsibility for ensuring that the company is accountable to its stakeholders and is operating in their best interests. Risk refers to the board's responsibility for identifying, assessing, and managing risks to the company's operations. Remuneration refers to the board's responsibility for ensuring that executive compensation is fair, transparent, and aligned with the company's long-term success.

The point at which the supply and demand curves intersect is known as the equilibrium. At the equilibrium
price, the quantity demanded will equal exactly the quantity supplied. There is no shortage or surplus of the
product. In the example shown in Figure 3.5, when the price is $15, consumers want to purchase 30 pizzas and
sellers want to make 30 pizzas available for purchase. The market is in balance.
A price higher than the equilibrium price will not be sustainable in a competitive marketplace. If the price of a
pizza were $20, suppliers would make 40 pizzas available, but the quantity of pizzas demanded would be only
20 pizzas. This would be a surplus, or excess quantity supplied, of pizzas. Restaurant owners who see that they
have 40 pizzas to sell but can only sell 20 of those pizzas will lower their prices to encourage more customers
to purchase pizzas. At the same time, the restaurant owners will cut back on their pizza production. This
process will drive the pizza price down from $20 toward the equilibrium price.

to spike; a temporary rise in gasoline prices can occur as a hurricane approaches the coastline. These types of
shocks are transitory in nature and do not represent underlying economic conditions.

producers, increases in the PPI can foreshadow increases in the CPI.

Unlike the CPI and the core inflation index, which are based on prices that households pay, the PPI captures price changes that occur prior to the retail level. Because it indicates rising costs to producers, increases in the PPI can potentially foreshadow increases in the CPI.

Instead of using a fixed basket of goods and services, the GDP deflator uses the entire Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to calculate inflation. This means that it takes into account the prices of all goods and services produced in an economy, not just a selected subset.

How Is GDP Measured?
GDP can be measured by adding up all of the items that are purchased in the economy. Purchases are divided
into four broad expenditure categories: consumption spending, investment, government spending, and net

qa_pairs.question: How is GDP measured in the economy?
qa_pairs.answer: GDP can be measured by adding up all of the items that are purchased in the economy. It is divided into four broad expenditure categories: consumption spending, investment, government spending, and net exports. Stages of the Business Cycle
The business cycle consists of a period of economic expansion followed by a period of economic contraction.
During the period of economic expansion, GDP rises. Employment expands as businesses produce more;
conversely, unemployment falls. Other measures of economic growth may include increased new business
starts and new home construction. The economy is said to be “heating up.” As the expansion continues,
inflation often becomes a concern.

An exchange rate is simply the price of a currency. If you live in the United States and are going on a trip to
Mexico, you will need pesos to pay for your food, hotel, and other items. You will need to purchase pesos.
Suppose that you go to your bank to purchase pesos. Suppose the bank tells you that it will cost $0.0625 to
purchase one Mexican peso. If you want to take 10,000 Mexican pesos with you on your trip, it will cost you
$625 to purchase the desired pesos.
In this example, the price of one peso is six and one-quarter cents. This price will often be written in the form

MXN is an abbreviation for the Mexican peso, and USD is an abbreviation for the US dollar. This price is known
as a currency exchange rate, or the rate at which you can exchange one currency for another currency.
Because this is the price you would pay to purchase Mexican pesos right now, it is known as the spot
exchange rate.

qa_pairs.question: What is the spot exchange rate?
qa_pairs.answer: The spot exchange rate is the price of a currency at the current moment. For example, if you are in the United States and want to purchase Mexican pesos, the spot exchange rate is the price you would pay to buy one Mexican peso right now.

qa_pairs.question: What does it mean for a currency to appreciate or depreciate?
qa_pairs.answer: When a currency appreciates, it becomes stronger and can buy more of another currency. For example, if the spot exchange rate for one US dollar is 0.0625 Mexican pesos and it increases to 0.065 Mexican pesos, the US dollar has appreciated because it can now buy more Mexican pesos. Conversely, when a currency depreciates, it becomes weaker and can buy fewer units of another currency. For example, if the spot exchange rate for one US dollar is 0.0625 Mexican pesos and it decreases to 0.06 Mexican pesos, the US dollar has depreciated because it can now buy fewer Mexican pesos.

Businesses that engage in international business face currency exchange rate risk. As exchange rates change,

example, will need to exchange the $20,000 for pesos to be able to pay its workers and other expenses in
pesos. How many pesos it will receive for $20,000 will change depending on the exchange rate. If the exchange

Firms that hold assets in a foreign country also face translation exposure. When a company creates its
financial statements, items are reported using one currency. As foreign exchange rates change, the value of
how items are reported on these financial statements can change. This type of risk is an accounting risk.
Economic exposure is the risk that a change in exchange rates will impact a business’s number of customers
and sales. For example, tourists have the option of spending a week-long vacation at a resort in the United
States or in Mexico. As the dollar appreciates, US citizens can exchange their dollars for more pesos, resulting
in their purchasing power going further at a Mexican resort. Because an appreciating dollar also means a
depreciating peso, it would mean that Mexicans who earn pesos will receive fewer dollars when they exchange
their pesos. A Mexican who wants to stay at a $200-per-night hotel in Colorado will need more pesos to pay for
the room when the peso depreciates. The depreciating peso will likely mean that more Mexicans will spend
their vacation week in Mexico, and fewer will vacation in the United States.

qa_pairs.answer: A falling CPI level indicates negative rates of inflation, or deflation. This means that the general price level of goods and services in an economy is decreasing over time.

3.1 Microeconomics
Microeconomics is the study of individual economic decision makers. In the marketplace, buyers and sellers
come together. The buyers are represented by a downward-sloping demand curve; lower prices are associated
with a larger quantity demanded. The sellers are represented by an upward-sloping supply curve; higher
prices are associated with a large quantity supplied. The point of intersection of the supply and demand curves
determines the equilibrium price and quantity.

3.2 Macroeconomics
Macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole. It focuses on broad issues such as inflation,
unemployment, and growth of production. The consumer price index is a common measure of inflation.
Unemployment equals the percent of the labor force that is without a job but looking for work. Gross domestic
product is a measure of the growth of production and growth of the economy.
3.3 Business Cycles and Economic Activity
The business cycle is the repeated pattern of the economy experiencing expansion, a peak, contraction, and a
trough. During the expansion, the economy is growing and real GDP is rising. During a contraction, also
known as a recession, the economy is slowing down.
3.4 Interest Rates
The interest rate is the rental price of money. The nominal interest rate is the quoted, or stated, rate of
interest. The real rate of interest equals the nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate. Lenders charge a
risk premium to compensate them for lending to higher-risk borrowers.

A foreign exchange rate is the price of a currency in terms of another currency. If a currency will purchase

qa_pairs.question: What is the GDP deflator and why is it important?
qa_pairs.answer: The GDP deflator is a measure of inflation tracked by the Bureau of Economic Analysis, intended to measure what GDP would be if prices did not change from one year to the next. It is important because it helps in understanding the rate of inflation in the economy, which can impact various economic indicators such as interest rates, consumer spending, and investment decisions.

qa_pairs.question: What is the law of demand and how does it affect the quantity of purchases?
qa_pairs.answer: The law of demand is the principle that the quantity of purchases varies inversely with price. This means that as the price of a good or service increases, the quantity demanded decreases, ceteris paribus (all other things being equal). This is because consumers tend to buy less of a good or service when its price increases, as they may perceive it as too expensive.

qa_pairs.question: What is macroeconomics and what are some of its key focus areas?
qa_pairs.answer: Macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole, focusing on unemployment, inflation, and total output. It examines broad trends and patterns in the economy, such as economic growth, business cycles, and fiscal and monetary policy. Other key focus areas include international trade, exchange rates, and government spending.

qa_pairs.question: What is microeconomics and how does it differ from macroeconomics?
qa_pairs.answer: Microeconomics is the study of individual economic units, such as households and firms, and their interactions. It focuses on the behavior of individual consumers and firms, and how they make decisions about consumption, production, and investment. In contrast, macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole, focusing on aggregate variables such as GDP, unemployment, and inflation. While microeconomics provides insights into individual behavior, macroeconomics uses these insights to understand and explain broader economic trends and patterns.

qa_pairs.question: What is macroeconomics and what are some of its main focuses?
qa_pairs.answer: Macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole. It focuses on understanding the economy's behavior at a broad level, particularly in terms of unemployment, inflation, and total output. This field of economics helps in analyzing the overall performance of an economy and the factors that influence it.

qa_pairs.question: What is microeconomics and what are its main focuses?
qa_pairs.answer: Microeconomics is the study of the economy at the individual level. It focuses on how individuals and businesses choose to allocate scarce resources. This field of economics delves into the decisions made by consumers, firms, and governments regarding the use of resources such as labor, capital, and raw materials.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between nominal and real interest rates?
qa_pairs.answer: The nominal interest rate is the quoted or stated interest rate. On the other hand, the real interest rate is the nominal interest rate minus the rate of inflation. This means that the real interest rate takes into account the effect of inflation on the purchasing power of money, providing a more accurate representation of the true cost of borrowing or the return on investment.

qa_pairs.question: What is the producer price index (PPI) and what does it measure?
qa_pairs.answer: The producer price index (PPI) is a measure of the prices that producers of goods and services pay for their supplies and raw materials. It helps in understanding the changes in the prices that businesses face when purchasing goods and services, which can impact their costs and ultimately their ability to sell their products at a profit.

qa_pairs.question: What is a recession and what characterizes it?
qa_pairs.answer: A recession is the part of the business cycle characterized by contraction. This means that during a recession, the economy experiences a decline in economic activity, as indicated by a decrease in gross domestic product (GDP), an increase in unemployment, and a decline in industrial production. Recessions can be caused by a variety of factors, including a decrease in consumer spending, a decline in business investment, or a financial crisis.

qa_pairs.question: What is the spot exchange rate and what does it represent?
qa_pairs.answer: The spot exchange rate is the price to immediately buy one currency in terms of another currency. It represents the current market value of one currency in terms of another, and it can fluctuate based on various factors such as interest rates, inflation rates, and political events.

qa_pairs.question: What is supply and what does it represent in economics?
qa_pairs.answer: Supply represents the quantity of a good or service that firms are willing to sell in the market during a given time period, ceteris paribus. This means that supply reflects the amount of a good or service that producers are willing to offer for sale at different prices, assuming all other factors remain constant.

qa_pairs.question: What is transaction exposure and what does it refer to?
qa_pairs.answer: Transaction exposure refers to the risk that the value of a business’s expected receipts or expenses will change as a result of a change in currency exchange rates. This risk can impact the financial health of a business, particularly if it has significant transactions in foreign currencies.

qa_pairs.question: What is translation exposure and what does it refer to?
qa_pairs.answer: Translation exposure refers to the risk that a change in exchange rates will impact the financial statements of a company. This risk arises when a company has assets or liabilities denominated in foreign currencies, and the value of those assets or liabilities changes as a result of fluctuations in exchange rates. This can impact the company's reported financial performance and may require adjustments to its financial statements.

qa_pairs.question: Who is the CFA Institute and what is its role?
qa_pairs.answer: The CFA Institute is a global association of investment professionals that aims to promote the highest standards of ethics, education, and professional excellence within the investment industry. It offers the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) designation, which is a respected credential for investment professionals worldwide.

qa_pairs.question: Why is the interest rate on a credit card so much higher than the interest rate on a car loan?
qa_pairs.answer: The interest rate on a credit card is typically much higher than the interest rate on a car loan due to several reasons. First, credit cards are unsecured loans, meaning they do not require collateral like a car loan does. This higher risk for the lender is reflected in a higher interest rate. Second, credit card interest rates are variable, meaning they can change over time based on market conditions, while car loan interest rates are often fixed. Lastly, credit card companies make a significant portion of their revenue from interest charges, so they have an incentive to set interest rates high.

qa_pairs.question: Has the Korean won appreciated or depreciated over the past year? Explain.
qa_pairs.answer: To determine if the Korean won has appreciated or depreciated over the past year, we need to compare the exchange rate between the Korean won and the US dollar from last year to this year. If the exchange rate has increased, meaning you can buy more Korean won with a US dollar now than you could last year, then the Korean won has appreciated. If the exchange rate has decreased, meaning you can buy fewer Korean won with a US dollar now than you could last year, then the Korean won has depreciated.

This increased money supply can lead to inflation as the same amount of goods and services are being bought with more money, causing prices to rise. This is a simplified explanation and the actual factors can be more complex, but this is one possible way the Federal Reserve's actions could lead to a higher rate of inflation than the United States has experienced over the previous few decades.

qa_pairs.question: List the types of unemployment presented in the video, giving an example of each type.
qa_pairs.answer: The video presents three types of unemployment: Cyclical unemployment, Structural unemployment, and Frictional unemployment. Cyclical unemployment occurs when there is a general downturn in the economy, such as a recession. An example of this could be the Great Recession of 2008-2009. Structural unemployment happens when there is a mismatch between the skills of the workforce and the needs of the economy. For instance, the shift from manufacturing to technology jobs in the 1980s and 1990s led to structural unemployment for many factory workers. Frictional unemployment is temporary and occurs when workers are between jobs or when there is a mismatch between a worker's qualifications and the job they are seeking.

qa_pairs.answer: Let's take the United States, Germany, and India as examples. Over the past decade, the unemployment rate in the United States has fluctuated between 4% and 10%, with a general downward trend. In Germany, the unemployment rate has been relatively low, ranging between 3% and 6%. India, on the other hand, has had a higher unemployment rate, ranging between 5% and 10%. A pattern that can be observed is that developed countries like the United States and Germany have lower unemployment rates compared to developing countries like India. The most prevalent type of unemployment in the United States seems to be frictional unemployment, as the economy is generally strong and there is a high demand for workers. In Germany, structural unemployment might be more prevalent due to the country's focus on specific industries like automotive and manufacturing. In India, both cyclical and structural unemployment might be prevalent due to the country's economic instability and the mismatch between the skills of the workforce and the needs of the economy.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between cash accounting and accrual accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: Cash accounting and accrual accounting are two methods used in accounting. Cash accounting records transactions only when cash is exchanged, while accrual accounting records transactions when they occur, regardless of when cash is exchanged. In cash accounting, income and expenses are recorded when cash is received or paid, whereas in accrual accounting, income is recorded when it is earned and expenses are recorded when they are incurred. The accrual method provides a more accurate picture of a company's financial position and performance over a period, making it more suitable for businesses with long-term commitments, such as loans or leases, and for businesses seeking external funding.

Cash-Basis Accounting
In business, cash is certainly important. In fact, it’s so important that it dictates one of two ways we can
account for our business transactions. The cash method is just as the name implies—it records transactions
only when cash flows. We track cash inflows and outflows as they occur. This method is most commonly used
by small businesses that deal primarily in cash transactions. The other method, called the accrual method,
records transactions when they occur, rather than waiting for cash to be accumulated. Using the accrual
method, we match cash inflows and the outflows required to generate them. We call this the matching
principle. This method is used by most publicly traded companies. In this chapter, you’ll explore both methods,
see how each impacts financial statements differently, note the role of timing in each method, and learn how
and when to record capital and expense transactions.

qa_pairs.question: What are the advantages of a company transitioning from cash-basis to accrual-basis accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: Transitioning from cash-basis to accrual-basis accounting can provide several advantages for a company like a beauty salon. One major advantage is that it allows for more accurate and timely financial reporting. With accrual-basis accounting, revenues and expenses are recorded when they are earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid. This means that the salon can get a clearer picture of its financial position at any given time, as it will be able to see the full extent of its revenues and expenses, even if it hasn't yet received or paid the cash. This can help the salon make more informed decisions about its business operations, such as forecasting future cash flow, managing its inventory, and planning for expenses. Additionally, accrual-basis accounting is often required by banks and other lenders, so transitioning to this method may make it easier for the salon to secure loans or lines of credit in the future.

qa_pairs.question: What are the disadvantages of a company transitioning from cash-basis to accrual-basis accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: While there are advantages to transitioning from cash-basis to accrual-basis accounting, there are also some potential disadvantages that a company like a beauty salon should be aware of. One major disadvantage is that accrual-basis accounting can be more complex and time-consuming than cash-basis accounting. This is because it requires tracking revenues and expenses that have been earned or incurred but not yet paid or received. This can be particularly challenging for a small business like a beauty salon that may not have a dedicated accounting department or staff. Additionally, accrual-basis accounting can lead to a delay in the reporting of cash flow, as revenues and expenses are recorded before they are actually received or paid. This can make it more difficult for the salon to manage its cash flow and may lead to cash flow problems if the salon is not careful. Finally, accrual-basis accounting can be more difficult to understand for those who are not familiar with accounting principles, which may make it more challenging for the salon to communicate its financial position to investors, lenders, and other stakeholders.

Ultimately, the decision to transition from cash-basis to accrual-basis accounting should be made in consultation with a qualified accountant or financial advisor who can help the salon weigh the pros and cons and make an informed decision based on its specific circumstances.

The Accounting Equation
It may be helpful to think of the accounting equation from a “sources and claims” perspective. Under this
approach, the assets (items owned by the organization) were obtained by incurring liabilities or were provided
by owners. Stated differently, every asset has a claim against it—by creditors and/or owners.
You may recall from mathematics courses that an equation must always be in balance. Therefore, we must
ensure that the two sides of the accounting equation are always equal. We will explore the components of the
accounting equation in more detail shortly. First, we need to examine several underlying concepts that form
the foundation for the accounting equation: the double-entry accounting system, debits and credits, and the
“normal” balance for each account that is part of a formal accounting system.
THINK IT THROUGH
The Accounting Equation

qa_pairs.question: What is the accounting equation in accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: The accounting equation in accounting is a fundamental equation that represents the balance of a company's financial statements. It states that Assets (items owned by the organization) equal Liabilities (debts owed by the organization) plus Owners' Equity (the residual interest in the assets after liabilities are subtracted).

qa_pairs.question: What is the 'sources and claims' perspective of the accounting equation?
qa_pairs.answer: The 'sources and claims' perspective of the accounting equation views assets (items owned by the organization) as being obtained by incurring liabilities (debts owed by the organization) or provided by owners. In other words, every asset has a claim against it—by creditors and/or owners.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of the double-entry accounting system?
qa_pairs.answer: The double-entry accounting system is a method of bookkeeping that records every financial transaction in at least two accounts. Its purpose is to ensure the accuracy and completeness of financial records by requiring that for every debit (an increase in an asset or expense account), there must be a corresponding credit (a decrease in a liability or owner's equity account).

qa_pairs.question: What are debits and credits in accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: In accounting, debits and credits are entries made in the accounting system to record financial transactions. A debit is an increase in an asset or expense account, while a credit is a decrease in a liability or owner's equity account. The double-entry accounting system requires that for every debit, there must be a corresponding credit to maintain the balance of the accounting equation.

qa_pairs.question: What is the 'normal' balance for each account in a formal accounting system?
qa_pairs.answer: In a formal accounting system, the 'normal' balance for each account is determined by the type of account. Asset, expense, and revenue accounts have a debit balance, meaning they increase when debited. Liability and owner's equity accounts have a credit balance, meaning they increase when credited.

qa_pairs.question: What is the purpose of creating a 'normal' balance for each account in a formal accounting system?
qa_pairs.answer: The purpose of creating a 'normal' balance for each account in a formal accounting system is to maintain the accounting equation, which is a fundamental principle in accounting. The accounting equation states that Assets (what you own) equal Liabilities (what you owe) plus Equity (the residual interest in the assets after liabilities have been subtracted). In other words, the normal balance for assets is a debit balance, while the normal balance for liabilities and equity is a credit balance. This helps ensure that the accounting system remains balanced and provides a clear picture of the financial status of the entity.

Double-Entry Accounting
Accounting is based on a double-entry accounting system, which requires the following:
•
Each time we record a transaction, we must record a change in at least two different accounts. Having two
or more accounts change will allow us to keep the accounting equation in balance.
•
Not only will at least two accounts change, but there must also be at least one debit and one credit side
impacted.
•
The sum of the debits must equal the sum of the credits for each transaction.
In order for companies to record the myriad of transactions they have each year, there is a need for a simple
but detailed system. Journals are useful tools to meet this need.
Debits and Credits

graphic representation of a general ledger account is known as a T-account. It is called this because it looks
like a “T,” as you can see with the T-account shown in Figure 4.3.

qa_pairs.question: What is the role of the revenue recognition principle in accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: The revenue recognition principle in accounting is used to determine when a sale has occurred and the revenue from that sale should be recognized. This principle relates to both current and future sales transactions, ensuring that revenue is recorded only when earned and is a reliable representation of the company's financial position.

qa_pairs.question: What is the role of the expense recognition principle in accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: The expense recognition principle in accounting is used to determine when a cost or expense has been incurred and should be recognized. This principle relates to both current and future purchase transactions, ensuring that expenses are recorded in the period in which they are incurred and are a reliable representation of the company's financial position.

qa_pairs.question: What is the relationship between ethics and revenue and expense recognition in accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: Ethics play a crucial role in revenue and expense recognition in accounting. Proper recognition of revenue and expenses requires honesty, transparency, and adherence to accounting principles. Ethical considerations are important to ensure that financial statements accurately reflect a company's financial position and performance, and that they are not manipulated to mislead stakeholders.

CONCEPTS IN PRACTICE
Ethics in Revenue Recognition
Because each industry typically has a different method for recognizing income, revenue recognition is one
of the most difficult tasks for accountants, as it involves a number of ethical dilemmas related to income
reporting. To provide an industry-wide approach, Accounting Standards Update No. 2014-09 and other
related updates were implemented to clarify revenue recognition rules. The American Institute of Certified
Public Accountants (AICPA) announced that these updates would replace US GAAP’s current industry-
specific revenue recognition practices with a principle-based approach, potentially affecting both day-to-
day business accounting and the execution of business contracts with customers.1 The AICPA and the
International Federation of Accountants (IFAC) require professional accountants to act with due care and to
remain abreast of new accounting rules and methods of accounting for different transactions, including
revenue recognition.
The IFAC emphasizes the role of professional accountants working within a business in ensuring the quality

Gift Card Revenue Recognition
Gift cards have become an essential part of revenue generation and growth for many businesses. Although
they are practical for consumers and are a low cost for businesses, navigating revenue recognition
guidelines can be difficult. Gift cards with expiration dates require that revenue recognition be delayed until
customer use or expiration. However, most gift cards now have no expiration date. So when do you
recognize revenue?
Companies may need to provide an estimation of projected (or deferred) gift card revenue and usage
during a period based on past experience or industry standards. There are a few rules governing reporting.

qa_pairs.question: What is the proper revenue recognition for gift cards with no expiration date?
qa_pairs.answer: For gift cards with no expiration date, revenue recognition should be based on an estimation of projected (or deferred) gift card revenue and usage during a period, which can be determined based on past experience or industry standards.

Expense Recognition
An expense is a cost associated with providing goods or services to customers. In our opening example, the
expenses that Chris incurred totaled $1,150 (consisting of $100 for brakes, $50 for fuel, and $1,000 for
insurance). You might think of expenses as the opposite of revenue, in that expenses reduce Chris’s checking
account balance. Likewise, expenses decrease the value of the business and represent the dollar value of costs
incurred to provide goods and services to customers for a given period of time.

qa_pairs.answer: Tangible assets are physical assets that can be seen or touched, such as buildings, equipment, and inventory. Intangible assets, on the other hand, are assets that cannot be seen or touched, such as patents, trademarks, and goodwill.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between expensing and capitalizing an item for a business?
qa_pairs.answer: Expensing an item means that the entire cost of the item is recorded as an expense in the current accounting period. Capitalizing an item means that the cost of the item is spread out over its useful life via depreciation, and the expense is recorded as a depreciation expense in each accounting period.

qa_pairs.question: What is the impact to net income of expensing versus capitalizing an item?
qa_pairs.answer: Expensing an item has a greater impact on net income in the current accounting period, as the entire cost of the item is recorded as an expense. Capitalizing an item and recording the expense as a depreciation expense over the useful life of the asset has a smaller impact on net income in the current accounting period, but the impact is spread out over multiple accounting periods.

qa_pairs.question: What is the definition of a fixed asset?
qa_pairs.answer: A fixed asset is any asset that is expected to be used by a business for more than one year and is not intended for resale. These assets are not intended for resale and are anticipated to help generate revenue for the business.

CONCEPTS IN PRACTICE
Estimating Useful Life and Salvage Value
Useful life and salvage value are estimates made at the time an asset is placed in service. It is common and
expected that the estimates are inaccurate due to the uncertainty involved in estimating the future.
Sometimes, however, a company may attempt to take advantage of estimating salvage value and useful life
to improve earnings. A larger salvage value and longer useful life decrease annual depreciation expense
and increase annual net income. An example of this behavior is Waste Management, which was disciplined
by the SEC in March 2002 for fraudulently altering its estimates to reduce depreciation expense and
overstate net income by $1.7 billion.4

qa_pairs.question: What is the double-declining-balance depreciation method and how does it differ from the straight-line depreciation method?
qa_pairs.answer: The double-declining-balance depreciation method is a complex depreciation method that accounts for both time and usage of an asset. Unlike the straight-line depreciation method, which spreads the depreciation expense evenly over the asset's estimated life, the double-declining method takes more expense in the first few years of the asset's life. It determines the percentage of depreciation expense that would exist under straight-line depreciation by dividing 100 percent by the estimated life in years. For example, a five-year asset would be 100/5, or 20 percent a year. A four-year asset would be 100/4, or 25 percent a year. To account for usage, the double-declining method doubles the straight-line percentage. For a four-year asset, this would be 25 percent multiplied by 2, resulting in 50 percent. For a five-year asset, this would be 20 percent multiplied by 2, resulting in 40 percent. This means that more depreciation is taken in the early years of the asset's life when it is typically more efficient and used more heavily.

qa_pairs.question: Why did McDonald's choose the method of depreciating assets, and do I agree with this choice?
qa_pairs.answer: McDonald's likely chose the double-declining balance method of depreciation due to its accelerated depreciation rate, which allows for a higher initial expense and a lower expense in later years. This method is often used for assets that lose value rapidly, such as equipment or vehicles. While this method can provide a more accurate reflection of the asset's declining value over time, it may not be as beneficial for tax purposes, as a higher initial expense can lead to a higher tax bill. As for whether I agree with this choice, it depends on the specific circumstances of McDonald's and the assets in question. If the assets are indeed losing value rapidly, then the double-declining balance method may be appropriate. However, if the assets are expected to maintain their value for a longer period, a different method, such as the straight-line method, may be more suitable.

When analyzing depreciation, accountants are required to make a supportable estimate of an asset’s useful
life and its salvage value. However, “management teams typically fail to invest either time or attention into
making or periodically revisiting and revising reasonably supportable estimates of asset lives or salvage
values, or the selection of depreciation methods, as prescribed by GAAP.”5 This failure is not an ethical
approach to properly accounting for the use of assets.
Accountants need to analyze depreciation of an asset over the entire useful life of the asset. As an asset
supports the cash flow of the organization, expensing its cost needs to be allocated, not just recorded as an
arbitrary calculation. An asset’s depreciation may change over its life according to its use. If asset depreciation
is arbitrarily determined, the recorded “gains or losses on the disposition of depreciable property assets seen
in financial statements”6 are not true best estimates. Due to operational changes, the depreciation expense
needs to be periodically reevaluated and adjusted.

Periodic reevaluation and adjustment of the depreciation expense are necessary due to operational changes.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a company's cash flow and its net income?
qa_pairs.answer: A company's cash flow refers to the inflow and outflow of cash within a business over a certain period. Net income, on the other hand, is a financial metric that represents the profit earned by a company after deducting all expenses from its total revenue. While a company with positive cash flow may have a net income, it's not necessarily true that a company with a net income will always have positive cash flow. This is because cash flow also includes changes in a company's working capital, investments, and financing activities, which are not necessarily reflected in the net income.

qa_pairs.question: What is double-entry accounting?
qa_pairs.answer: Double-entry accounting is a method of bookkeeping that records every financial transaction in at least two accounts, a debit account and a credit account. This method ensures that the total debits always equal the total credits for each transaction, maintaining the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

qa_pairs.question: What is the expense recognition principle?
qa_pairs.answer: The expense recognition principle states that expenses should be recognized in the accounting period in which they are incurred and can be measured reliably. This means that expenses are recorded when they are consumed or used up, regardless of when cash is actually paid.

qa_pairs.question: Why is ethics an important concept pertaining to revenue and expense recognition principles?
qa_pairs.answer: Ethics are important in revenue and expense recognition principles because they help ensure that financial statements are accurate and reliable. By adhering to ethical principles, companies can avoid manipulating revenue and expense recognition to mislead investors and stakeholders about their financial performance.

qa_pairs.question: What is the revenue recognition principle?
qa_pairs.answer: The revenue recognition principle states that revenue should be recognized in the accounting period in which it is earned and can be reliably measured. This means that revenue is recognized when it is realized or realizable, and earned, regardless of when cash is actually received.

qa_pairs.question: What is the difference between a tangible and an intangible fixed asset? List common examples of each.
qa_pairs.answer: A tangible fixed asset is a physical asset that can be touched, seen, or felt, such as buildings, machinery, vehicles, and furniture. An intangible fixed asset, on the other hand, is an asset that does not have a physical form, such as patents, trademarks, copyrights, and goodwill. Common examples of tangible fixed assets include buildings, machinery, and vehicles, while common examples of intangible fixed assets include patents, trademarks, and copyrights.

qa_pairs.question: How is the cost of a fixed asset recorded and recognized over time?
qa_pairs.answer: The cost of a fixed asset is recorded as an asset on the balance sheet and is recognized over time through depreciation or amortization. Depreciation is the gradual reduction in the value of a tangible fixed asset over its useful life, while amortization is the gradual reduction in the value of an intangible fixed asset over its useful life. The cost of a fixed asset is allocated to the accounting periods in which the asset is used, reducing the asset's book value and increasing the expense on the income statement.

qa_pairs.question: Have companies really experienced a loss if they expense a large sum of cash to invest in equipment or another fixed asset?

However, it is important to note that the company has not actually lost the value of the asset, as it still owns the asset and can use it to generate future revenues. The delineation between expensing and capitalizing an asset is a matter of accounting convention and does not necessarily reflect the economic reality of the transaction.

qa_pairs.question: Is the depreciation process ethical?
qa_pairs.answer: The depreciation process is a common accounting practice used to allocate the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life. Whether it is ethical or not is subjective and depends on one's perspective. Some argue that it is ethical because it allows businesses to account for the gradual decline in the value of an asset over time, which is more accurate than recognizing the entire cost in the year of purchase. Others argue that it hides the true cost of business, making financial statements less transparent. For instance, if a business depreciates an asset too quickly, it may understate its expenses and overstate its profits, which could potentially mislead investors and creditors. On the other hand, if a business depreciates an asset too slowly, it may overstate its expenses and understate its profits, which could also mislead investors and creditors. Therefore, it is crucial for businesses to use conservative estimates when determining depreciation rates to ensure financial transparency.

qa_pairs.question: Is the cash flow the same in timing and amount as the expense a business recognizes?
qa_pairs.answer: No, cash flow and expenses do not always coincide in timing and amount. When a business incurs an expense, it may not immediately pay for it in cash. For example, a business may purchase office supplies on credit, meaning it will pay for them at a later date. Similarly, a business may recognize an expense in its accounting records before it actually pays for it. For instance, a business may recognize wages expense in the accounting period in which the services are performed, even though it may not pay the employees until a later date. This discrepancy between the timing of cash outflows and expense recognition is known as the timing difference, and it is one of the reasons why a business's cash flow and its expenses may not be the same.

qa_pairs.question: Are the key components necessary to calculate profit or loss the same as the elements necessary to calculate cash flow?
qa_pairs.answer: No, the key components necessary to calculate profit or loss are not the same as the elements necessary to calculate cash flow. Profit or loss is calculated by subtracting total expenses from total revenues, while cash flow is calculated by adding or subtracting cash inflows and outflows from a business's cash account. Expenses and revenues are accounting concepts that are recognized in the income statement, while cash inflows and outflows are actual transactions that are recorded in the cash flow statement. Therefore, while some expenses and revenues may be included in the cash flow statement, not all expenses and revenues are included, and vice versa.

Now that we have gone to all the work to carefully assemble a classified balance sheet, what do we use it for?
The answer lies within the accounting equation itself. Think of the accounting equation from a “sources and
claims” perspective. Under this approach, the assets (items owned by the organization) were obtained by
incurring liabilities or were provided by owners. Stated differently, every asset has a claim against it—by
creditors and/or owners. The balance sheet shows us what the firm has (its assets), who owns them (equity),
and who the firm owes (its liabilities).

Limitations of the Balance Sheet
The balance sheet is indeed a very helpful financial statement, but it also poses challenges. First, assets on the
balance sheet, under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), are recorded at historical cost.
Historical cost is simply the cost paid for the item at the time it was purchased. Changes in market value of big-
ticket items like land or buildings are not reflected in the balance sheet. Land remains at historical cost, and
depreciable items like buildings are reflected at their current book value (historical cost less accumulated
depreciation). If the asset has appreciated over time, the higher market value of the assets would not be seen
on the balance sheet.
Estimates are another limitation of the balance sheet. Items on the balance sheet such as allowance for
doubtful accounts and allowance for bad debt are based on estimates. The useful lives for calculating
depreciation is another common estimate. If these estimates are incorrect, the net value of the asset can be
under- or overstated.
